title: Three Verbs Under One Roof
label: ch:ge-sein-drei-wurzeln
canDo: I can put the German verb for “to be” into the past, and say why its forms look like three unrelated words — because they are.

payoff.summary: The past of sein is the tidy half of the verb: one stem war-, ordinary endings, and ich war identical to er war. The chapter teaches those four cells one at a time and then answers the question the present tense raised — bin, ist and war come from three different Proto-Indo-European verbs, which is called suppletion, and it survives because the words you never have to guess at are the words analogy never reaches.
payoff.note: Split out of the hand-written chapter 16, which carried the present, the past and the sein-perfect in one chapter and could not hold them inside maxNewAtomsPerChapter at one atom per grammar cell. The payoff claims all seven of this chapter's atoms: the practice lesson drills the four past cells and then asks for the three roots, the name suppletion, and the reason the verb was never tidied up.
